description:
## Мрія ("Mriya") means "dream" in Ukrainian.

We are a team of four curious creators and problem-solvers based in Vancouver, Canada, with Ukrainian roots. United by our passion for space, science, technology, and innovation, we combine creativity, engineering, and data-driven thinking to explore challenges, build practical solutions, and turn ambitious ideas into reality.
summary:
We developed **NISAR Northwest Passage SAR Ice Navigator**, an interactive maritime decision-support platform that transforms real 2026 NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) Level-2 Geocoded Covariance (GCOV) data into Polar Code routing intelligence for ships transiting the Canadian Arctic Archipelago.

To address the "Dancing with the SARs" challenge, our automated Python pipeline ingests 2026 NISAR L-band (24 cm) dual-polarization (HHHH/HVHV) and single-polarization (VVVV) scenes over Barrow Strait, applies coastline land-masking, and classifies sea ice into Open Water, First-Year Ice, and hazardous Multi-Year/Ridged Ice via cross-polarization volume scattering. An interactive Streamlit and Folium dashboard samples these regional radar mosaics along deep-water NORDREG shipping corridors to compute vessel-specific transit feasibility, delay hours, and excess fuel burn, paired with a seasonal before/after swipe comparator and visual SAR physics modules.

This capability is vital as Arctic maritime traffic grows while optical satellites remain blinded by storm clouds and months of polar night, and shorter C-band radar scatters off surface snow. NISAR’s L-band radar penetrates snowpack in all weather, helping mariners avoid multi-year ice ridges, cut emissions, and prevent environmental disasters in fragile polar waters.
details:
What It Does & How It Works

NISAR Northwest Passage SAR Ice Navigator is an interactive maritime decision-support platform that transforms real 2026 NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) Level-2 Geocoded Covariance (GCOV) data into Polar Code routing intelligence for ships transiting the Canadian Arctic Archipelago.

The platform operates through a four-stage end-to-end pipeline:

  1. Automated Orbital Ingestion (pipeline/load_real_scenes.py): Queries NASA’s Alaska Satellite Facility (ASF) Vertex API (asf_search) for 2026 NISAR L2_PR_GCOV HDF5 granules over Parry Channel and Barrow Strait—ingesting both Dual-Polarization (DHDH: HHHH + HVHV) swaths for multi-year ice detection and Single-Polarization (NASV: VVVV) sea-ice monitoring passes across summer open-water and autumn freeze-up windows.
  2. Radiometric Calibration, Land Masking & Geometric Reprojection: Extracts terrain-flattened covariance layers (/science/LSAR/GCOV/grids), converts linear backscatter ($\gamma^0$) to decibels ($\gamma^0_{\text{dB}} = 10 \log_{10}\gamma^0$), rasterizes Arctic island coastlines (Cornwallis, Somerset, Devon, and Bathurst Islands) to NoData so rocky terrain never triggers false ice alarms, and warps polar UTM grids (EPSG:32615/32616) into EPSG:4326 via rasterio.warp for pixel-accurate alignment with satellite basemaps.
  3. 3-Tier Polarimetric Hazard Classification & Mosaicking: Segments ocean pixels into Tier 1: Open Water (specular low backscatter), Tier 2: First-Year Ice (moderate surface scattering, low cross-pol depolarization), and Tier 3: Multi-Year / Ridged Ice (strong HVHV volume scattering from brine-drained air pockets and pressure-ridge keels), then stitches adjacent swaths using rasterio.merge into regional seasonal composites.
  4. IMO Polar Code Tactical Routing Engine (app/routing.py & app/main.py): Samples 350+ georeferenced waypoints along end-to-end deep-water Canadian Coast Guard NORDREG corridors (Primary NORDREG Deep-Water Mainline via Parry Channel and M'Clure Strait vs. Southern Tactical Bypass via Peel Sound and Victoria Strait) and evaluates sampled ice concentrations against the selected vessel’s structural rating (Standard Cargo, Polar Class 6, or Heavy Icebreaker) to calculate an operational verdict (NAVIGABLE, CAUTION, or BLOCKED), effective speed, transit delay, and excess fuel burn.

Key Benefits

  • All-Weather, 24-Hour Polar Night Visibility: Unlike optical sensors (Sentinel-2, MODIS) that fail during winter darkness and persistent Arctic cloud cover, NISAR’s active L-band radar images sea-ice conditions day or night through severe storm decks.
  • Sub-Snow Structural Ice Detection: NISAR’s 24 cm L-band wavelength penetrates dry Arctic snowpack to reveal the true sea-ice structure beneath, overcoming the snow-grain scattering limitations of shorter 5.6 cm C-band radars.
  • Immediate Bridge-Ready Risk Quantification: Converts complex radar decibel arrays into clear operational metrics—hull safety status, delay hours, and fuel burn penalties tailored to the vessel’s ice class.
  • Lightweight & Low-Bandwidth Deployment: Compresses multi-gigabyte HDF5 orbital products into self-contained GeoTIFF mosaics and a JSON manifest (~2.4–5 MB), enabling fast cloud hosting and low-bandwidth shipboard access.

Intended Impact

  • Preventing Maritime Disasters in Fragile Arctic Ecosystems: As retreating summer sea ice drives increased commercial traffic through the Northwest Passage, reliable detection of multi-year ice ridges reduces the risk of hull breaches, vessel entrapment, and catastrophic fuel spills in remote northern waters.
  • Reducing Fuel Burn & Black Carbon Emissions: By identifying open-water leads and lower-resistance southern tactical bypasses (such as Peel Sound), ships avoid heavy icebreaking bottlenecks, cutting fuel consumption and Arctic black carbon deposition.
  • Democratizing Polarimetric SAR Telemetry: Bridges the gap between specialized Earth-observation radar physics and practical maritime navigation for captains, logistics planners, and students.

Tools, Coding Languages, Software & Hardware Used

  • Programming Language: Python 3
  • SAR & Geospatial Libraries: asf_search (NASA ASF Vertex API client), h5py (HDF5 covariance extraction), rasterio (UTM-to-WGS84 reprojection, coastline masking, and multi-pass rasterio.merge mosaicking), geopandas, shapely, and pyproj
  • Scientific Computing & Plotting: numpy, scipy, matplotlib
  • Web Application & Mapping Stack: streamlit, folium, streamlit-folium, custom dark-mode inline SVGs, and Esri World Imagery basemap tiles
  • NASA & Open Data Sources: NASA Earthdata / NISAR Level-2 GCOV products, Canadian Coast Guard NORDREG corridor geometries, Natural Earth Arctic coastline boundaries, and Wikimedia Commons open-licensed vessel and sea-ice reference photography
  • Hardware & Deployment: Ubuntu Linux workstation, Git/GitHub (mriya-lab/nisar-nwp-navigator), and Streamlit Community Cloud

How Our Project Is Creative

  • Fusing Electromagnetic Physics with Naval Architecture: Rather than stopping at a raw radar heatmap, we coupled polarimetric backscatter classification directly with IMO Polar Code hull limits—visualized through custom technical hull-belt SVG cross-sections paired with real Arctic vessel photography.
  • 4-Tab Interactive Storytelling: Alongside the Tactical Route Map, we built a split-screen Before / After Swipe Comparison slider (contrasting August open water against late-October freeze-up mosaics), a SAR Physics & Briefing lab with an interactive polarimetric signature simulator and HHHH vs. HVHV decision-boundary plot, and a System Architecture & Data Pipeline blueprint tab.
  • Resilient Dual-Mode Engine: Built the data layer to run seamlessly on live reprojected NISAR GeoTIFFs while retaining a calibrated synthetic fallback engine so the platform remains testable anywhere.

Key Factors Our Team Considered

  • High-Latitude Map Projection Distortion: At 74.7° N in Barrow Strait, native polar UTM grids (EPSG:32615/32616) are rotated relative to true North. We explicitly warped raster pixels into EPSG:4326 prior to web rendering so radar coastlines match satellite basemaps pixel-for-pixel.
  • Eliminating Land-Scattering False Positives: Rocky Arctic islands exhibit high radar roughness (> -10 dB) that mimics multi-year sea ice. We integrated coastline polygon masking to exclude landmasses from sea-ice hazard statistics.
  • Wind-Roughened Water vs. Cross-Pol Discrimination: Wind-driven capillary waves on summer open water can elevate co-polarized (VV/HH) backscatter; we accounted for mode differences between single-pol (NASV) and dual-pol (DHDH) acquisitions when calibrating seasonal thresholds.
  • Maritime Bathymetry & Deep-Water Routing: Plotted end-to-end NORDREG waypoints strictly within navigable deep-water channels (Parry Channel, Barrow Strait, Peel Sound, Victoria Strait, and M'Clure Strait) with zero island crossings.
